Whenever someone asks about my dissertation topic and I answer “Ottoman tents,” their first thought is usually of Anatolian nomads, or perhaps ruthless Turkish conquerors and their vast armies. For this reason, I always show them a photo, to make clear that the kinds of tents I work on are actually appliquéd, embroidered, fringed, gilt, sequined, and otherwise extraordinarily ornate silken palaces. My dissertation examines these luxurious imperial tents used by the sultans in the last century or so of Ottoman rule (from the end of the 18th century to the beginning of the 20th). This period was a time of modernization in the Ottoman Empire, which witnessed the advent of photography and railroads, as well as changes in imperial aesthetic tastes, which have been described as Turkish “Baroque” or “Rococo,” and which likewise appeared in fabric architecture.
With the generous support of several grants including the Rackham Merit Fellowship, the Rackham International Research Award, the Rackham Graduate Student Research Grant, and a nine-month research fellowship at the Research Center for Anatolian Civilizations in Istanbul—altogether I spent two summers (2013 and 2015) chasing tents across Europe, and a full academic year (2015-2016) in Istanbul to study the tents, archives, and architecture in the Ottomans’ capital city.
Ottoman tents found their way to Europe through various means over the centuries—from being won in battle and taken as war booty or simply purchased from Istanbul, or in some cases, European artisans made their own tents in the style of the Ottoman sultans’. While in Europe those two summers, I studied tents in various national and palatial museums, local collections, and historic chateaus in Vienna, Warsaw, Kraków, Tarnów, Kórnik, Berlin, Dresden, Karlsruhe, Lviv, Stockholm, Madrid, and Athens. Each place presented its own challenges, and its own rewards, and of course, more than a few surprises. Whenever a museum was generous enough to allow me access to their “backroom” (whether a dusty storeroom or a large warehouse off-site from the museum proper) I felt a rush of adrenaline as the appliqued, embroidered, and gilt fabric was unfurled before me. Then would begin the process of furious note taking, photographing, and sketching its every detail and overall character.
But nothing could have prepared me for my research experience at the Military Museum in Istanbul. I had worked there before—in summer 2013—but at that time I was given access only to the library and the tents that were installed in the galleries. This year, however, after having built a relationship with the institution over the intervening years (helped along with gifts of homemade sweets), I was allowed access to their tent depot. I was shocked to discover that the Military Museum housed upwards of two hundred specimens, which the curatorial staff is currently in the midst of cataloguing. To put that number in perspective, the tents that are in the Topkapı Palace collections number around thirty.
The magnitude of this discovery hit me only when I saw row upon row of rolled up tents stacked into mountains of heavily decorated cloth. My first thought was of Hanger 51 in the final scenes of Indiana Jones and the Lost Ark. I knew then that this project might in fact be a lifetime of work, and that my dissertation is only the beginning. content:Speaker assistant says: Biryani: A Dish with a Rich Legacy and Cultural Significance

Biryani is a flavorful, spicy, and aromatic dish that is popularly known as the king of South Asian cuisine. It originated in Persia and was introduced in India by Mughal invaders. Over time, it became a staple dish of the Indian subcontinent and is now served in various forms across different regions.

Ingredients

Biryani is a rice-based dish that is usually made of basmati rice, spices, and meat or vegetables. The spices typically include cumin, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, bay leaves, and saffron. Depending on the region and family traditions, additional ingredients such as tomato, onion, garlic, ginger, nutmeg, and mace may also be added.

Meat-based biryanis are usually made with chicken, beef, lamb, or fish, while vegetable biryanis use various vegetables like carrots, peas, cauliflower, potatoes, and eggplant. Some biryanis also include dry fruits, such as raisins and cashews, that add a sweet and crunchy flavor to the dish.

Preparation

The preparation of biryani is an elaborate and time-consuming process that involves several steps. Usually, the rice is first washed, soaked, and then boiled with whole spices and aromatics, such as cinnamon sticks, bay leaves, and cardamom pods. Once cooked, the rice is layered with the meat or vegetables that have been cooked separately in a rich and flavorful sauce.

The meat or vegetable layers are flavored with saffron, fried onions, and sometimes dry fruits before being covered with a tight-fitting lid to allow the flavors to meld together. Biryani is typically served hot with side dishes like raita (spiced yogurt), chutney, and salad.

Cultural Significance

Biryani holds a significant place in the culinary traditions of the Indian subcontinent, and it is consumed in a wide range of social contexts, from family gatherings to weddings and religious events. It symbolizes prosperity, royalty, and hospitality and is often served to guests as a sign of respect and goodwill.

It is also believed that the dish has its roots in hospitality traditions that date back to the Mughal era. According to historical accounts, the Mughals were known for their elaborate feasts, and biryani was a key part of their banquet tables. To this day, biryani is an essential part of luxurious meals and celebrations.

In conclusion, biryani is a dish that reflects the fusion of various cultures and traditions in the Indian subcontinent. Its preparation, ingredients, and cultural significance vary across regions and communities, but it remains an enduring symbol of hospitality, prosperity, and indulgence. Whether it's a bowl of spicy chicken biryani from Hyderabad or a vegetarian biryani with aromatic spices from Kashmir, this dish never fails to tantalize taste buds and is sure to leave a lasting impression on those who try it. context:Food tradition keywords: biryani, dish, South Asian cuisine, spices, rice, Mughal, hospitality, cultural significance, ingredients, preparation, meat, vegetables, raita, chutney, saffron, Hyderabad, Kashmir tags: food tradition, regional cuisine, food history, cultural context, culinary exploration

1. World on Fire: How Exporting Free Market Democracy Breeds Ethnic Hatred and Global Instability:
- Overall Rating: 4.0
- Review: This original book deserves attention and I would recommend it to economists other than political scientists. The author is a professor of law at Yale, but her background does not come up in the book. That is good for the general reader. The first lines begin with a dramatic personal experience, a homicide, in her family back in the Philippines, a wealthy Chinese family in a destitute social environment. After that, the book develops the idea that market-dominant minorities in several countries, with no continental exception, with the support of an undemocratic political system in many cases, have generated resentments in the majority of the population, who have in turn developed a strong, even violent, distaste for a market economy, globalization (whatever is the content in that label), and ethnic backlash. Amy Chua comes to the conclusion that democracy can be inimical to the interests of market-dominant minorities. However, democracy means different things to different peoples, as she correctly points it out. Market-dominant minorities see democracy as a means for protecting themselves from the tyranny of the oppressed majority and the conservation of the status quo. Oppressed majorities see democracy as a means for the redistribution of wealth and equal opportunities, even as a springboard for human development. In the social and ethnic contexts described by Chua, rapid democratization can lead to unwanted results. To prove her thesis, Prof. Chua gives many examples taken from around the world. In certain cases, her examples are overstretched, especially when it tackles the US and other countries. In others, the book becomes repetitive. But the bottom line seems to be correct and deserves a closer look. The book does not contain a general theory that is applicable to all cases. However, Prof. Chua applies it too generously even when that is only a minor blip in a more complex situation. All in all, it is a great book.

2. The Penguin Historical Atlas of the Vikings (Hist Atlas):
- Overall Rating: 4.0
- Review: Vikings, which stands for "raiders," were strong shipbuilders and sailors, and their fame became soon known to their victims around Europe. Their brutality was recorded in chronicles from their victims (literate clergymen), and in part, their ill fame is probably the result of bad press of that time.

History needs maps. A historical atlas is very useful if a reader wants to keep track of all Viking raids and pillages around the coasts of northern Europe, but also as far as today's Russia and Central Asia. Vikings gave the name to Russia, being Rus the name Finns gave to Swedish Vikings in that area, which means "oarsmen." So this historical atlas provides plenty of information through maps and entertaining captions that help to understand how far-reaching Viking influence was. However, this atlas, as a previous reviewer has noted, is too centered on Viking presence in British islands and Ireland.

At the beginning of the 10th century, Charles III of France gave Normandy (the land of Norse) to the Vikings, who, in turn, offered their allegiance. These settled Vikings became known as Normans, who took part in new adventures: William, the Duke of Normandy, led the conquest of England, Robert the Guiscard seized Sicily from Muslims in the Mediterranean, and took part in the Crusades. This by-product of the Viking saga is almost completely left out.

All in all, this atlas provides a visual history of Vikings that is appropriate and easy to read for students and the general reader. Recommended to all who share an interest in Medieval history of Northern Europe.

3. The Closing of the Western Mind: The Rise of Faith and the Fall of Reason:
- Overall Rating: 5.0
- Review: An accessible story of how the West gradually abandoned its rational and critical thinking. At some point (for reasons of state or for fear of uncertain times), religion superseded reason and Aristotle was forgotten. The book presents the main actors and events in this process under a unified view. Simple and informative at the same time. Good reading for all. context:World on Fire: How Exporting Free Market Democracy Breeds Ethnic Hatred and Global Instability keywords: World, Market, Democracy, Vikings, History, Faith, Reason, Book tags: Culture, Risk Management, Ethics

Many people treat the speed limit as though it’s a required minimum, but it’s important to remember that it’s a maximum speed. You are in no way required to drive the posted speed. Determine your own speed (as long as it’s below the speed limit!) and stick with what you’re comfortable with.
Be sure that you always have a small winter survival kit packed for emergencies. This kit should contain things like a snow scraper, a small shovel to dig yourself out, a bag of salt to melt ice if you park in a slick spot, a few hand warmers, and a few nonperishable snacks.
A huge mistake that drivers fall victim to during the holiday season is over consuming alcohol during holiday parties. Give yourself a maximum at the beginning of the night and stick to it. Whether it’s just one drink or two drinks, just remind yourself that it’s what’s reasonable for you and don’t let anyone talk you into more.
If the unthinkable should happen – a breakdown or accident in the middle of winter – do not leave your car. The car is the warmest place that you have available in the middle of the cold. Instead use your cell phone to call for help and stay put!

content:Speaker assistant says: If you do experience a breakdown or accident in the middle of winter, it’s important to stay calm and follow a few key steps to ensure your safety. First, turn your hazard lights on to alert other drivers of your situation. If you have a roadside emergency kit, use it to put out warning devices such as flares or reflective triangles to further alert oncoming traffic.

If the weather conditions are particularly cold and harsh, it’s important to stay warm and dry. Make sure you have warm clothing available in your car, such as a coat, gloves, and hat. Turn your car off to conserve fuel, but turn on the engine and heater for 10-15 minutes every hour to stay warm. If you have blankets or sleeping bags available, use them to further insulate yourself and stay warm.

If you’re unable to get help on your own, use your cell phone to call for assistance. Make sure to tell the dispatcher where you are and what happened. If you’re in a particularly remote area, it may take emergency services longer to get to you, so be prepared to wait. Keep your phone charged and don’t waste the battery on non-essential apps or games.

In the event that you need to leave your car to get help, make sure you are visible to other drivers. Wear bright clothing or a reflective vest and stay as close to your car as possible. Stay on the shoulder and do not attempt to cross a busy roadway.

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly, here are some fun games that coaches can use to promote skill development for young soccer players:

1. Sharks and Minnows: The coach designates a few players as "sharks," and the rest are "minnows." The minnows start on one end of the field and must dribble to the other end without being tagged by the sharks. If a minnow is tagged, they become a shark.

2. Four Corners: The coach sets up four cones in each corner of the field and designates each corner with a number (1, 2, 3, or 4). Players must dribble their ball to a corner when the coach calls out a number. The last player to arrive at the correct corner is out.

3. Dribble tag: All players dribble a ball in a confined area. One player is designated as "it" and must try to tag other players by touching their ball with their foot. If a player's ball is tagged, they switch roles with the player who tagged them.

4. Capture the Flag: Divide players into two teams and place a cone or flag at each end of the field. Players must dribble their ball to the opposing team's flag and knock it over before returning to their own side.

5. Red Light, Green Light: The coach serves as a traffic light and calls out "green light" to signal players to dribble their ball forward, and "red light" to signal players to stop. Players who don't stop in time are out.

Winning may be the short-term goal of the coach, players, and parents, but it should not come at the expense of long-term development.

1. Drink water regularly: Start drinking water regularly days before the race to ensure you are well-hydrated. During the race, aim to drink small sips of water every 15-20 minutes.

2. Use sports drinks: Sports drinks can help replace the electrolytes you lose through sweat, which can help prevent dehydration. Look for sports drinks with sodium and potassium levels appropriate for your body.

3. Monitor your urine color: If your urine is darker than pale yellow, it’s an indicator that you may be dehydrated. Aim for clear or slightly pale yellow colored urine.

4. Take salt tablets: In hot weather, running causes a lot of sweating which causes loss of sodium. You can take salt tablets to replace the loss of sodium.

5. Eat water-rich fruits: Eating watermelon, grapes, strawberries, peaches or any other water-rich fruit can help keep you hydrated.

6. Pay attention to the weather: If the weather is hot, make sure to bring extra fluids to sip on during your run.

7. Plan your water stops: Know the locations of water stops along the racecourse beforehand, and plan your hydration strategy accordingly. context:confidence keywords: hydration, race, electrolytes, dehydration tags: hydration, nutrition, stamina

content:Speaker assistant says: Yes, here are some tips to improve your running technique:

1. Posture: Keep an upright posture, with your shoulders relaxed and your head level. Look forward, not down at the ground.

2. Foot strike: Aim to land midfoot or forefoot, avoiding heel-striking. This helps reduce the impact on your joints and promotes a more efficient running style.

3. Cadence: Aim to have a cadence of around 180 steps per minute. Count the number of times one of your feet hits the ground in 30 seconds, then double it. This will help you avoid over-striding and lead to a smoother and more efficient running style.

4. Arm swing: Keep your arms at your sides or bent at a 90-degree angle, swinging naturally and purposefully. Avoid crossing your arms over your body, as this can disrupt your balance and waste energy.

5. Breathing: Focus on deep belly breathing and try to sync your breathing with your steps. Inhale for three to four steps, hold for one or two, then exhale for three to four steps.

6. Warm up: Take a few minutes to warm up before your run with some dynamic stretches and drills, such as high knees, butt kicks, and leg swings.

7. Consistency: Regularly practicing good technique will help make it a natural part of your running style. Pay attention to your form during your runs and make adjustments as necessary.

Remember, it may take time and practice to perfect your running technique, so be patient with yourself and enjoy the process. context:This document provides guidance on improving running form, focusing on posture, cadence, and stride mechanics to enhance efficiency and reduce injury risk. keywords: posture, running technique, cadence tags: posture, running technique, cadence, breathing, stride, injury

content:Speaker assistant says: Planning and executing a training program for running events can be a daunting task, especially for beginners. However, with proper planning and guidance, anyone can train effectively for a 5k, half marathon, marathon, or ultramarathon. Here's a comprehensive guide to help you plan and execute your training program.

Step 1: Set Your Goals

Before starting any training program, it's essential to define your goals. Ask yourself what you want to achieve from the training program. Do you want to finish the race? Do you want to improve your time or distance? Once you have defined your goals, you can tailor your training program to achieve those objectives.

Step 2: Develop a Training Schedule

After identifying your goals, the next step is to develop a training schedule. A training schedule outlines the number of weeks you have to train before the race and the number of workout sessions you'll need in those weeks. Here's a sample training schedule for different types of running events:

5k: 8 weeks

Half marathon: 16 weeks

Marathon: 20 weeks

Ultramarathon: 24 weeks

The training should start with shorter distances and lower intensities and gradually increase over time.

Step 3: Workouts

Your training program should include the following workouts: 

1) Long Runs: Long runs are a critical component of any training program for 5k, half marathon, marathon, or ultramarathon. They build endurance and help train the body to run for extended periods. 

2) Tempo Runs: These runs are faster-paced than long runs and are designed to improve your lactate threshold, which helps you run faster for longer periods. 

3) Interval Runs: These are short-distance, high-intensity runs with recovery periods and help improve your speed and running economy. 

4) Cross-training: Include activities such as swimming, cycling, and strength training in between running sessions to avoid injury and build overall fitness.

Step 4: Recover between Training Sessions

Recovery between training sessions is essential to avoid injuries and ensure that your body is ready for the next workout. Here are some tips to help:

1) Stretching: Stretching improves flexibility, reduces muscle soreness, and prevents injury. 

2) Rest: Give your body a chance to recover after every workout. Take a day or two off each week, depending on the intensity of your training. 

3) Nutrition: Proper nutrition before and after your workout is necessary to fuel your body and aid recovery. 

4) Sleep: Get enough sleep to allow your body to recover and repair.

Step 5: Nutrition, Hydration, and Gear

A proper nutrition plan is necessary to fuel your body for training and the race. Ensure you take the following into account:

1) Carbohydrates: Carbohydrates provide energy and should make up a significant portion of your diet. 

2) Protein: Protein is essential for muscle recovery and should form a significant portion of your diet. 

3) Healthy Fats: Ensure you consume healthy fats as they provide energy and help with muscle recovery.

Hydration is essential in any running training program. Ensure that you drink enough water and consume electrolytes to aid hydration. 

Investing in the right gear is essential when planning a training program. Ensure that you have the right shoes, socks, and clothing to help prevent injuries and improve your performance.

Step 6: Strategies for Injury Prevention and Mental Preparation

Injury prevention is crucial during your training program. Here are some tips to help you avoid injuries:

1) Warm-up: Always warm up before a workout to prepare your muscles and joints for the activity. 

2) Listen to Your Body: Listen to your body and rest if you feel any pain or discomfort during training. 

3) Cross Training: Cross-training is essential in reducing the impact of running on your body and injury prevention. 

Mental preparation is an essential component of any training program. Here are some tips:

1) Visualization: Visualize yourself running the race successfully before the race day. 

2) Positive Thinking: Always stay positive and avoid negative thoughts. 

3) Relaxation: Relax and remain calm before the day of the race.

Conclusion:

In summary, planning and executing a training program for running events requires a comprehensive approach that covers different aspects of training, hydration, nutrition, gear, injury prevention, and mental preparation. Use this guide to develop an effective training program that will help you achieve your goals and complete your race successfully. context:A comprehensive guide to planning and executing a training program for running events, particularly 5k, half marathon, marathon, and ultramarathons. content:Speaker assistant says: Yes, hill workouts are an excellent way to build strength and endurance for running events, and they can be incorporated into your training program regardless of the distance you are preparing for. Here's some additional information on how to incorporate hill workouts into your training program for different types of running events.

1) 5k Hill Workouts:
When preparing for a 5k, hill workouts can help you build strength and improve your speed. Incorporate 4-5 hill repeats into your training program once a week, increasing the number of repeats gradually each week. You can start by finding a gradual hill with a moderate incline and running up it at a steady pace. Recover by jogging slowly or taking a walk down the hill before repeating the process.

2) Half Marathon Hill Workouts:
Hills can be incorporated into your long run program when preparing for a half marathon. Find a route that includes a hill with a moderate incline and run up it at a steady pace once every mile for the duration of your long run. Start with a single hill and gradually increase the number of hills over time.

3) Marathon Hill Workouts:
For marathon training, hill workouts are an essential component since most marathons have hilly terrain. Find a hill with a moderate incline and incorporate it into your tempo runs. You can start with 2-3 hill repeats in the middle of your tempo run, gradually increasing the number of repeats each week.

4) Ultramarathon Hill Workouts:
Incorporating hill workouts into your ultramarathon training program is essential since you will encounter hills over long distances. Find a hill with a moderate incline and run up and walk down it to recover. Start with 5-6 repeats and gradually increase the number of repeats each week.

Here are some additional tips for incorporating hill workouts into your training program:

- Warm-up before starting the hill workout to prepare your muscles and joints.
- Wear appropriate shoes that provide good grip and traction when running on hills.
- Focus on maintaining proper form when running uphill - lean slightly forward, maintain a fast cadence, and lift your knees high.
- Recover properly between hill repeats by walking briskly or jogging slowly down the hill.
- Increase the number of hill repeats gradually each week to avoid over-exertion and injury.

content:Speaker assistant says: For many runners, strength training is an afterthought, if it is even considered at all. However, incorporating strength training into a running routine can greatly enhance overall performance and prevent injury.

Muscle groups to target:
- Glutes: The glutes play a major role in a runner's stride as they are responsible for extending the hip and stabilizing the pelvis. Exercises such as squats, lunges, and hip bridges can greatly improve glute strength.
- Core: A strong core is essential for maintaining proper running form and preventing injury. Planks, crunches, and Russian twists are just a few examples of exercises that target the core muscles.
- Hamstrings: The hamstrings work in conjunction with the glutes to extend the hip and promote forward propulsion. Deadlifts, hamstring curls, and step-ups can help strengthen this muscle group.

Types of exercises:
- Bodyweight exercises: Squats, lunges, planks, and push-ups are all effective bodyweight exercises that can be done anywhere and require no equipment.
- Free weights: Dumbbells and kettlebells can be used for exercises such as deadlifts, lunges, and overhead presses.
- Resistance bands: Resistance bands are a versatile and portable option for strength training. They can be used for exercises such as clamshells and lateral walks.
- Plyometrics: Plyometric exercises, such as box jumps and jumping lunges, can help improve explosive power and running economy.

Improving running form:
Strength training can help improve running form by addressing muscle imbalances and weaknesses. A strong core can improve posture and prevent excessive forward lean, while strong glutes can help maintain proper stride length and reduce the risk of IT band syndrome. Additionally, exercises such as single-leg squats and balance drills can address any imbalances between the left and right sides of the body.

Preventing injuries:
Strength training can help prevent injuries by promoting proper biomechanics and addressing muscle imbalances. By strengthening the muscles that support the knees, hips, and ankles, runners can reduce the risk of common running injuries such as plantar fasciitis, shin splints, and patellofemoral pain syndrome.

Enhancing overall performance:
Strength training can enhance overall performance by improving running economy, increasing stride length, and promoting faster turnover. By developing power and explosiveness in the muscles, runners can also improve their ability to sprint and tackle hills.

In conclusion, incorporating strength training into a running routine can greatly enhance overall performance and prevent injury. By targeting specific muscle groups and incorporating a variety of exercises, runners can improve running form, prevent injuries, and enhance overall performance. So, don't forget to hit the weights in addition to pounding the pavement. context:For many runners, incorporating strength training into their routine can significantly improve overall performance and reduce the risk of injury. It involves targeting specific muscle groups to address imbalances and weaknesses that can hinder progress. keywords: strength training, running, glutes, core, hamstrings, running form, injury prevention, performance enhancement tags: running technique, form, injury prevention, performance, cadence

How strength training can improve endurance and speed:

1. Increases Muscular Endurance:
Strength training increases the endurance of muscles, which means you can run faster and longer. It is because, when you strengthen the muscle fibres and increase the number of connections between muscle fibres and nerves, it reduces the amount of energy required to contract those muscles thereby increasing the endurance and efficiency of your muscle groups during a run.

2. Enhances Running Economy:
Running economy plays a crucial role in running performance as it measures the amount of oxygen required to run at a particular pace. So, the less oxygen you require, the faster and better you can run. Strength training enhances the neuromuscular connections and efficiency of the muscles, which translate to better and faster running economy.

3. Increases Anaerobic Threshold:
Strength training helps in increasing the anaerobic threshold, which is the point where your muscles start producing lactic acid. It means your muscles can work harder for a longer duration, meaning you will experience less exhaustion while running, thereby increasing both your endurance and speed.

4. Increases Explosive Power:
Strength training also increases your explosive power, which is the ability to suddenly produce a burst of energy, commonly required while hill climbing or sprint finishes. Strength training increases the recruitment of muscle fibres during the initial phase of muscle contraction, improving explosive power and increasing speed.
